notes: A partial answer is useful: the single most common qualifying route with a national range would let the whole path be built and measured.
The two major parties are equally unrepresented here, so an answer must cover why they are always on the ballot without hardcoding their names.
question: A new party founds itself in an ordinary save, with members and a platform, and can never appear on a ballot, because ballot access is not represented for any party including the two major ones. So: (1) what are the qualifying routes a party actually has in American states — petition signatures, a share of a previous statewide vote, registered affiliates, a filing fee — and which of these is worth representing; (2) what are the thresholds, in the shape of a rule that can be expressed per state and drawn nationally where a state has not been read, which is how this repository already handles unresearched jurisdictions; (3) what does a party lose access for, and how long does access last once earned; (4) should access be per office, per state, or both; and (5) what should a player be able to do about it — is founding or qualifying a party something a player acts on, or something they watch happen?

sourcesChecked.source: src/simulation/living-world/party-evolution.ts read in full, and two ordinary saves run forward
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Establishes that party founding occurs unprompted and that ballot status is a stub with no callers. Settles that this is a content question, not a systems one. Contains no threshold, because none was ever authored.

sourcesChecked.source: The repository's existing rule that unresearched jurisdictions get a realistic range drawn nationally, stable per state, with real law overriding
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Gives the shape any answer must take. Does not supply the national spread for ballot access, which nobody has read.

title: How a party earns ballot access, so the third party the game already founds can matter
usableAnswer: The qualifying routes worth representing, with thresholds expressible per state. A retention and loss rule. A position on per-office versus per-state. And a clear statement of which of these is a rule the game may assert nationally and which must be read state by state, since this repository does not let a generated default stand in for real law where real law is known.
whyItMatters: Measured 2026-09-22 at main 62368c1e. WHAT EXISTS: a full party-evolution system, 1969 lines, with founding, splits, mergers, renames, platform changes and dissolution — and it runs on its own: a brand new party founded itself inside two years of one Kentucky save with no player involvement. THE ONE MISSING LINK: partyBallotStatusAt() takes no arguments and returns the literal string not-represented, with a comment saying no registered committee or ballot access is represented; it has zero callers. So the founding is real and can never reach a voter. THE SMALLEST HONEST CHANGE: give that function a party and a state, and one rule to answer with. WHAT A PLAYER WOULD SEE: the new party in their county on a ballot line, or a stated reason it is not there — which is the owner's third-party question, and half of it already happens.
